blocks.prompt: The Fish Where the Dad Has the Babies
blocks.text: A seahorse is a fish, but it swims standing straight up. A little fin on its back beats so fast that you can hardly see it. Even so, a seahorse is slow. The smallest kind is the slowest fish in the sea. It would take a whole hour to cross a bathtub. A seahorse has no teeth. It has a long snout, and it sucks up its food like a straw. The dad is the one who has the babies. The mom puts her eggs into a pouch on his front. He keeps them safe. Weeks later, he pushes out tiny seahorses, no bigger than a grain of rice.

blocks.prompt: The Fish That Swims Standing Up
blocks.text:
A seahorse does not look like a fish, but it is one. It has gills. It has fins. It is covered in bony rings instead of scales, which makes it feel like a tiny suit of armor.

Almost nothing about a seahorse works the way you would expect. It swims upright, pushed along by one small fin on its back that beats about thirty times a second. Even with all that effort, it barely moves. The dwarf seahorse is the slowest fish anyone has ever measured. It travels about five feet in an hour.

Being slow is fine, because a seahorse does not chase anything. It wraps its tail around a blade of seagrass and waits. Its two eyes move on their own, so one can look up while the other looks down. When a tiny shrimp drifts past, the seahorse snaps its head forward and sucks the shrimp in through its snout. The whole thing is over in less than the blink of an eye.

The strangest part comes last. Seahorse dads get pregnant. The mom lays her eggs inside a pouch on the dad's belly, and he carries them until they hatch.

blocks.prompt: Built Wrong, Working Perfectly
blocks.text:
Everything about a seahorse looks like a mistake. It is a fish that cannot swim well. It has no teeth and no stomach. Its body is ringed with bony plates instead of scales. And the males, not the females, are the ones who get pregnant. Somehow, none of this is a problem.

Start with the swimming. A seahorse holds itself upright and moves by fluttering a single fin on its back, roughly thirty beats every second. That buzzing fin produces almost no speed. The dwarf seahorse, measured carefully by scientists, covers about five feet in an hour, which makes it the slowest fish on record.

A slow fish should starve. Instead, a seahorse anchors itself. Its tail is prehensile, meaning it can grip, and it curls around a stem of seagrass and holds on while the current pushes food past. Its eyes swivel independently, watching two directions at once.

Then comes the ambush. A seahorse eats copepods, specks of shrimp so alert that they can feel water moving toward them and flick away. So the seahorse cheats. The shape of its head barely disturbs the water in front of the snout, creating a quiet zone the copepod never feels. The seahorse drifts in, then snaps its head up and slurps. The strike is faster than you can blink, and it usually works.

The lack of a stomach explains the rest. Food rushes through a seahorse so quickly that it has to eat almost constantly, hunting all day long.

And the pregnancy is real, not a nickname. The female deposits her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly. He fertilizes them, feeds them oxygen, and adjusts the fluid inside until it matches the sea. Weeks later, he pumps hundreds of finished seahorses out into the water.

blocks.prompt: The Slowest Hunter in the Sea
blocks.text:
A seahorse is a fish that has abandoned almost every advantage a fish has. It cannot outrun anything. It has no teeth to bite with and no stomach to store a meal in. Its body is stiff, ringed in bony plates, and held upright like a chess piece. Every one of those apparent failures turns out to be a trade.

Consider speed. The seahorse's only real engine is the dorsal fin on its back, which flickers around thirty times a second and produces almost nothing. The dwarf seahorse holds the record as the slowest fish ever measured, at roughly five feet an hour. But a seahorse is not trying to travel. It is trying to disappear. It grips a stem of seagrass with a prehensile tail and becomes, for all practical purposes, part of the plant.

That tail is stranger than it looks. Most animal tails are round in cross section. A seahorse tail is square. When engineers built models of both and crushed them, the square tail proved harder to break and better at gripping, and it snapped back into shape afterward. Nature arrived at a design a mechanical engineer would recognize.

The hunting is where the trade pays off. Seahorses eat copepods, which are among the twitchiest animals alive. A copepod can sense water pushing ahead of a predator and escape in a few thousandths of a second. So the seahorse does not push water. The curve of its snout and head creates a pocket of nearly still water directly ahead, and the seahorse eases into striking range through that quiet pocket. Then its head pivots upward and its snout draws the copepod in like a pipette. In tests, dwarf seahorses succeeded on roughly nine out of ten strikes, an extraordinary rate for any hunter.

The missing stomach forces the pace. Food passes through so fast that a seahorse must feed for most of the day, picking off prey one at a time.

Then there is the pregnancy, which is not a figure of speech. The female transfers her eggs into a sealed pouch on the male's abdomen. Inside, he fertilizes them, supplies oxygen through a network of blood vessels, feeds them, and slowly shifts the saltiness of the pouch fluid toward seawater so the newborns will survive the outside. He then labors, sometimes for hours, and releases them. Fewer than one in a hundred will reach adulthood.

blocks.prompt: Forty Ways to Be a Bad Fish
blocks.text:
Every schoolbook definition of a fish is a list the seahorse quietly breaks. Fish are fast; the seahorse is the slowest swimmer in the ocean. Fish are flexible; the seahorse is a rigid tube of bony rings, held vertical, moved by a fin that flutters like an insect's wing and gets it almost nowhere. Fish are, with famous exceptions, not the sort of animal where the father gives birth. And yet there are more than forty species of them, from a pygmy seahorse the length of your fingernail to an Australian big-belly seahorse the length of your forearm, and they have been doing this for millions of years. The seahorse is not a badly built fish. It is a fish built for a job nobody else applied for.

Biologists group seahorses in the genus Hippocampus, from the Greek for horse and sea monster, alongside their relatives the pipefish and sea dragons. Their strange body plan appears to have followed the spread of seagrass meadows across shallow tropical seas. In open water, speed is survival. In a meadow, speed is pointless and stillness is everything. So the seahorse traded its engine for an anchor.

The anchor is the tail, and it is the first place the engineering shows. Nearly every prehensile tail in nature, from a monkey's to a chameleon's, is round in cross section. A seahorse's tail is built from square, stacked bony plates. When researchers printed both shapes and tested them, the square version gripped better, absorbed crushing force without shattering, and slid back into alignment afterward. Roundness is elegant; squareness is armor that still bends. A predator can bite a seahorse's tail and the tail survives.

The second place the engineering shows is the head, and it is the reason a slow animal does not starve. Seahorses eat copepods, tiny crustaceans with a reflex that borders on unfair: they detect the bow wave of an approaching mouth and fire themselves away within milliseconds. Almost nothing catches them reliably. The seahorse does, because it never makes a bow wave. The narrow snout and the shape of the head above it leave a zone of nearly motionless water directly in front, and the seahorse creeps forward inside that silence. When it is close enough, the head snaps upward and the snout inhales. The whole capture takes roughly a thousandth of a second. Watch a dwarf seahorse hunt and it will hit about nine strikes out of ten, which is a better record than a shark, a wolf, or a hawk.

It has to be. A seahorse has no stomach at all. Food falls through its digestive tract so quickly that almost the only thing a seahorse does is eat, picking off prey after prey for most of the daylight hours.

Then there is the pregnancy, which biologists mean literally. The female produces the eggs and deposits them, through a tube, into a sealed pouch on the male's abdomen. What happens next is not simple babysitting. He fertilizes the clutch, grows blood vessels through the pouch wall to deliver oxygen, secretes nutrients into it, and gradually raises the salt content of the pouch fluid until it matches the sea outside, so that his young are not shocked the moment they leave him. He is running a placenta. After several weeks, he goes into labor, and hundreds of fully formed seahorses are pumped out into the current. Fewer than one in a hundred will survive to breed.

The irony is that this careful animal is being emptied out of the ocean faster than it can replace itself. Seagrass meadows are disappearing under sediment and development. Seahorses are hauled up as bycatch in shrimp trawls by the tens of millions each year, dried, and sold for traditional medicine and souvenirs. Every species was placed under international trade controls in 2004. A fish that survived by being impossible to notice is being taken by nets that were never even looking for it.
